extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and readers of Blackstone studying English constitutional and public law
extracted.subtask_description: Expository legal treatise material (Blackstone) describing rules, principles, and historical practices governing the monarchy, succession, royal family, councils, and prerogative in English law. Useful for learning the legal standards and historical statutes that define royal rights and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of succession (Act of Settlement limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The title to the crown is at present hereditary but conditional: the inheritance vested in the princess Sophia and limited to such heirs of her body who are Protestant members of the Church of England and married to none but Protestants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains change in the 'common stock' of descent (now Princess Sophia) and that succession is hereditary but restricted by statute/settlement; historical context of the 1688/Act of Settlement adjustments to descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper constitutional notion of succession (moderate/limited heredity)
rubrics_metrics.description: True constitutional notion of the right of succession lies in a due medium between election by the people and divine indefeasible hereditary right; extremes (pure election or absolute divine right) are destructive of society's ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance: the best constitution interweaves hereditary succession with the liberties of subjects; the passage argues for balance rather than extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queen regnant's powers equal to a king
rubrics_metrics.description: A queen regent, regnant, or sovereign (one who holds the crown in her own right) has the same powers, prerogatives, rights, dignities, and duties as if she had been a king (declared by statute 1 Mar. I. st. 3. c. 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Queen Mary(s), Elizabeth, Anne. Statutory confirmation referenced; practical implication that a reigning queen exercises full sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal status and capacities of the queen consort (feme sole)
rubrics_metrics.description: The queen consort is a public person, exempt and distinct from the king, and is treated in many respects as a feme sole: able to purchase and convey lands, make leases, grant copyholds, take grants from the king, have separate courts and officers, sue and be sued alone, possess separate property and dispose of it by will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the reason given by Sir Edward Coke: the king should not be troubled with his wife's domestic affairs; traces the privilege back to Saxon times; cites authorities (Co. Litt., Finch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Queen consort exemptions and general equality before law
rubrics_metrics.description: The queen enjoys certain minute prerogatives and exemptions (e.g., pays no toll, not liable to amercement in any court) but, except where law expressly declares exemption, she stands on the same footing as other subjects and is the king's subject, not his equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Roman maxim 'augusta legibus soluta non est' to note limits; specific exemptions are exceptional and statutory or ancient practice-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queen-gold (aurum reginae) perquisite and rules of collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Queen-gold is an ancient perquisite of the queen consort: a tenth part additional on voluntary offerings or fines of ten marks or upwards given to the king for certain royal favours; it becomes a debt of record to the queen by recording the fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists exceptions when no payment is due (aids/subsidies granted in parliament, fines imposed by courts, voluntary presents without consideration, grants diminishing crown revenues); gives historical examples and notes on neglect and revival attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigned demesne revenues for the queen and their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically certain rents/reservations from crown demesnes were appropriated to the queen for specific uses (e.g., to buy wool, oil for lamps, or to furnish apparel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Domesday and pipe-roll entries detailing reservations; explains historical practice and examples of expenditures for the queen's attire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal fish (whale) division rule
rubrics_metrics.description: On taking a whale (a royal fish), the division is: the king has the head, and the queen the tail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient, whimsical perquisite explained as furnishing the queen's wardrobe with whalebone; authorities from Bracton, Britton, Fleta cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treason protections for the queen consort and specified royal persons
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (25 Edw. III) to compass or imagine the death of the queen consort is high treason; to violate or defile the queen consort also amounts to high crime; similarly, compassing the death of the prince of Wales or violating the chastity of the prince or princess royal is high treason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains rationale: protection of succession and prevention of bastardizing heirs; cites examples and statutory sources; notes distinction for queen dowager.

rubrics_metrics.name: Husband of a queen regnant is a subject (liable to treason) but treated differently regarding conjugal fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: The husband of a queen regnant is the queen's subject and may be guilty of high treason against her, but in relation to conjugal fidelity he is not subjected to the same penal restrictions as a husband of a queen consort would be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: the infidelity of a queen consort may bastardize heirs; the infidelity of a husband to a queen regnant cannot produce the same danger to succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queen dowager rights and marriage constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A queen dowager (widow of the king) enjoys most privileges of a queen consort, is entitled to dower even if alien-born, is not the object of the same treason protections as the queen consort, but cannot marry without special licence from the king on pain of forfeiting lands and goods; upon remarriage she does not lose her regal dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites authorities (2 Inst. 18, Co. Litt.) and historical examples (Katherine, queen dowager of Henry V; queen of Navarre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special regard and precedence for the prince of Wales and royal children
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince of Wales (heir apparent), his consort, and the princess royal receive special protection and precedence by law (e.g., statutes making compassing their death or violating their chastity high treason) and enjoy precedence before all peers and public officers by statute 31 Hen. VIII. c. 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes hereditary titles (duke of Cornwall by inheritance, prince of Wales by creation) and historical judge opinion (1718) that the king has care of grandchildren's education and marriages during their father's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence rules for younger royal children
rubrics_metrics.description: Younger sons and daughters of the king (not in immediate succession) receive precedence before all peers and public officers but are otherwise less regarded by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains statutory source (31 Hen. VIII. c. 10) and the limits of their legal regard compared with the immediate heirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of councils belonging to the king and their subject-matter specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: The king is assisted by diverse councils: (1) the high court of parliament; (2) the peers of the realm as hereditary counsellors (in or out of parliament); (3) the judges of the courts of law, as council for legal matters; and (4) the privy council as the principal council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that 'king's council' must be particularized 'secundum subjectam materiam' — when the subject is legal, the king's council means his judges; provides historical instances of peer conventions and use of each council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peers as hereditary counsellors: functions and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Peers are created 'ad consulendum' and 'ad defendendum regem': to give counsel to the king and to defend the realm; they may be called to advise in parliament or in councils when no parliament sits; enjoy privileges such as freedom from arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records historical practice of assemblies of peers for advice; notes the right of each peer to demand audience of the king and the legal consequences when that right was obstructed (impeachment example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges as king's council for legal matters (interpretation rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the king's council is referred to with legal subject-matter, the term is to be understood as the king's judges of his courts of justice; statutes and books of law frequently adopt this interpretation (e.g., 14 Ed. III. c. 5; 16 Ric. II. c. 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives example of importing papal bulls where offenders were to be brought before 'king and his council' meaning judges; emphasizes necessity to particularize council by subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privy council: appointment, composition, duties (oath), powers, jurisdiction limits, qualifications, privileges, and dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Privy counsellors are appointed by the king's nomination without patent, take an oath of office (seven articles: advise the king with discretion, for public good, secrecy, avoid corruption, help execute resolutions, withstand opposers, perform duties of a true counsellor), and possess powers to inquire into offences and commit offenders for trial but not to punish; jurisdictional limits exclude matters of property (court of starchamber dissolved), though appeals in plantations/admiralty and lunacy/idiocy remain; qualifications require natural-born subjects and compliance with security and test oaths (Act of Settlement restricts those born abroad); privileges include statutory protection against attempts on their lives; dissolution is at the king's pleasure but statute 6 Ann. c. 7 keeps council for six months after the demise of the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical variation in size and structure noted (anciently ~12, later limited to 30, then indefinite); statutory examples (16 Car. I. c. 10; 3 Hen. VII. c. 14; 9 Ann. c. 16) and illustrative incidents (stabbing of Harley) provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of the king (coronation oath) — govern by law, execute judgment in mercy, maintain established religion and clergy rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The coronation oath (statute 1 W. & M. st. 1. c. 6) requires the sovereign to promise to govern according to statutes and laws and customs, to cause law and justice in mercy to be executed, and to maintain the laws of God, the true profession of the gospel, and the Protestant reformed religion established by law, and to preserve rights and privileges of bishops and clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of oath transcribed in the text; characterized as the express 'original contract' between sovereign and people; statutory confirmation and historical continuity noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's fundamental constitutional duty: govern according to law (limits on prerogative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The king must govern his people according to the decrees of the laws; the sovereign is subject to God and the law — 'the law maketh the king' — and is bound by oath at coronation to observe laws; statutes (12 & 13 W. III. c. 2) declare the laws of England the birthright of the people and require sovereigns to administer government according to those laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Bracton and Fortescue to support the claim; lays foundation for limiting the king's prerogative and for the notion that prerogative is necessary but constrained by law and the original contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's prerogative: necessity and lawful bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The king's prerogative is necessary for the support of society and the maintenance of civil order, but it must be marked out in its important instances and restricted so clearly that the king cannot exceed them without the consent of the people or without violating the original contract between prince and subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefatory normative claim to chapter on prerogative: invites minute consideration of necessity, extent, and restrictions of prerogative, asserting that discussion of prerogative is a proof of genuine freedom.
